titleStmt.title: The Status and Future of Consciousness Research

bibl.title: The Status and Future of Consciousness Research

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: The two entangled obstacles of consciousness research - how to measure consciousness, and what counts as a neural correlate of it.
span.quote: One major obstacle for consciousness research is the lacking consensus of how to optimally measure consciousness empirically.

span.label: critique
span.quote: One major obstacle for consciousness research is the lacking consensus of how to optimally measure consciousness empirically.

span.label: measurement of consciousness and its neural correlates
span.quote: Historically, the attempt to “measure” consciousness has unfolded as a debate between direct and indirect approaches.

span.label: review
span.quote: As it will be argued below, consciousness research may face problems in the future that are currently less debated but which are logical extensions of the challenges above.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Any objective measure must be calibrated against something already known to track consciousness, and that anchor is a subjective report - so the weaknesses of introspection are re-imported into every objective method
span.quote: Furthermore, in order to arrive at any one particular objective method, one must have “calibrated it” to something else in order to know that this particular behavior can be considered a measure of consciousness—and not something else.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Objective measures work only under an unstated assumption that the threshold for a correct response coincides with the threshold for having the experience, which is what makes them fallible as measures of awareness
span.quote: For one thing, objective measures must assume that the “threshold” of giving a correct response is the same as the “threshold” of having a subjective experience of the same content

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Empirical consciousness science arose less from new neuroscience technology than from an openness that let philosophical, cognitive and neuroscientific questions, methods and arguments be integrated
span.quote: This development was of course influenced by the technological advancements in neuroscience during those decades, but more important and fundamental was a new openness to interdisciplinary integration of research questions, methods and arguments.

span.label: The two obstacles are one problem: you cannot look for the correlates of something without first fixing how you will measure it
span.quote: This challenge clearly relates to the first as one needs to apply a measure of consciousness in order to identify its correlates.

span.label: An objective measure has to be calibrated against something, and the only available something is a subjective report - so the weaknesses it was designed to avoid come back in through the calibration
span.quote: This would typically involve associating a subjective report with a particular behavior—a process by which one would “import” all the weaknesses related to subjective reports that one tried to avoid in the first place (Overgaard, 2010 ).

span.label: No-report paradigms do not escape this, because associating a behavioural marker with experience in the first place requires introspection
span.quote: However, and as mentioned above, the only way one may associate a phenomenon as nystagmus with conscious experience is by the direct use of introspection (to establish the “correlation”) (Overgaard and Fazekas, 2016 ).

span.label: Objective measures also assume the threshold for a correct response coincides with the threshold for experiencing the content, which is an assumption and not a finding
span.quote: For one thing, objective measures must assume that the “threshold” of giving a correct response is the same as the “threshold” of having a subjective experience of the same content (Fu et al., 2008 ; Timmermans and Cleeremans, 2015 ).

span.label: One proposed resolution of the prefrontal-versus-occipital dispute is that both are right about different things, because there are two kinds of consciousness
span.quote: Block ( 2005 ) argues that there may be two neural correlates of consciousness: One relating to phenomenal consciousness (the “early” activations), and one relating to access consciousness (the “late” activations).

span.label: Existing evidence cannot adjudicate the metaphysical question, because it fits every position equally
span.quote: Existing data, however, seems to fit easily into every theoretical understanding of this problem.

span.label: The paper explicitly presents its list of challenges as a selective sample rather than a complete survey of the field's problems.
span.quote: The challenges highlighted above obviously only represent a few of the many scientific and theoretical issues that scientists in this area face.

span.label: The field's central term is used without its ambiguity being examined
span.quote: Although it is rarely debated what we mean with a “neural correlate of consciousness,” most experiments aim to identify the minimal neural activations that are sufficient for a specific content of consciousness (Chalmers, 2000 ).

span.label: There is still no universally accepted measure of the thing being studied
span.quote: Whereas we still have no universally accepted measures of consciousness, much progress has been made with regards to how one may grasp the content of an experience in the context of an experiment.

span.label: The patient comparisons that would settle levels of consciousness are confounded by lesion variability and reorganisation
span.quote: most brain injured patients have many different lesions and, consequently, massive reorganization, which makes comparisons very difficult

span.label: Some patients classified as unconscious appear not to be, so the contrast group is unreliable
span.quote: Some experiments indicate that not all such patients are unconscious (Owen et al., 2006 ), and—at the same time—most brain injured patients have many different lesions and, consequently, massive reorganization, which makes comparisons very difficult.

span.label: The label 'no-report paradigm' names nothing new, since every purely objective paradigm is already without report
span.quote: Essentially, all paradigms using objective measures only are without report, so in a certain sense, paradigms labeled “no-report paradigms” have not introduced anything new.

span.label: neural correlate of consciousness - of CONTENT: the minimal activations sufficient for one specific conscious content
span.quote: Although it is rarely debated what we mean with a “neural correlate of consciousness,” most experiments aim to identify the minimal neural activations that are sufficient for a specific content of consciousness (Chalmers, 2000 ).

span.label: neural correlate of consciousness - AS SUCH: what distinguishes being awake from asleep or dead, not tied to any content
span.quote: Contrary to this, other scientists are preoccupied with finding neural correlates of consciousness “as such”—i.e., neural correlates that mark the difference between being dead, asleep, awake, etc., and which are not content-specific in the sense above.

span.label: measuring consciousness - DIRECT: the subject reports their own experience, with the known limits of self-report
span.quote: Direct approaches, at least intuitively, are the most informative as participating experimental subjects here simply report about their own experiences.

span.label: measuring consciousness - INDIRECT: performance on a task stands in for experience, which avoids self-report and imports a threshold assumption instead
span.quote: Experiments on consciousness that are based on objective measures—the “indirect” approach—typically involve asking subjects to choose between alternatives, e.g., in forced-choice tasks.

span.label: early activations - as the correlate of phenomenal consciousness, which is the currently favoured reading
span.quote: According to most recent reviews and articles, evidence is lending support toward the latter view (Andersen et al., 2016 ; Koch et al., 2016 ; Hurme et al., 2017 ).

span.label: early activations - as PRECONSCIOUS: information not yet conscious, which is the opposite reading of the same data
span.quote: Nevertheless, proponents of the opposite view—that consciousness is associated with prefrontal cortex activity—argue that “early” activations in fact represent preconscious states—i.e., information that is not yet conscious (e.g., Lau and Rosenthal, 2011 ).

span.label: builds-on → Overgaard and Fazekas (2016)
span.quote: However, and as mentioned above, the only way one may associate a phenomenon as nystagmus with conscious experience is by the direct use of introspection (to establish the “correlation”) (Overgaard and Fazekas, 2016 ).

span.label: critiques → no-report paradigms as a solution to the measurement problem
span.quote: However, and as mentioned above, the only way one may associate a phenomenon as nystagmus with conscious experience is by the direct use of introspection (to establish the “correlation”) (Overgaard and Fazekas, 2016 ).

span.label: critiques → the position that objective measures alone can settle questions about consciousness
span.quote: For one thing, objective measures must assume that the “threshold” of giving a correct response is the same as the “threshold” of having a subjective experience of the same content (Fu et al., 2008 ; Timmermans and Cleeremans, 2015 ).

span.label: supports → Block's two-correlates proposal as a reading of the prefrontal/occipital dispute
span.quote: According to other perspectives, this debate is partially misunderstood.

span.label: extends → the REF-CON model, on which there need be no universal correlate at all
span.quote: According to the REF-CON model of consciousness, subjective experience is intrinsically related to a particular kind of “strategy” that makes information available for action (Overgaard and Mogensen, 2014 ; Mogensen and Overgaard, 2017 ).

span.label: subjective report —contrasted-with→ objective measures
span.quote: Historically, the attempt to “measure” consciousness has unfolded as a debate between direct and indirect approaches.

span.label: objective measures —causes→ introspection
span.quote: This would typically involve associating a subjective report with a particular behavior—a process by which one would “import” all the weaknesses related to subjective reports that one tried to avoid in the first place (Overgaard, 2010 ).

span.label: no-report paradigms —same-as→ objective measures
span.quote: Essentially, all paradigms using objective measures only are without report, so in a certain sense, paradigms labeled “no-report paradigms” have not introduced anything new.

span.label: forced-choice tasks —operationalised-as→ objective measures
span.quote: Experiments on consciousness that are based on objective measures—the “indirect” approach—typically involve asking subjects to choose between alternatives, e.g., in forced-choice tasks.

span.label: Perceptual Awareness Scale —operationalised-as→ subjective report
span.quote: Proponents of the “direct” approach have attempted to develop precise and sensitive scales to capture minor variations in subjective experience, e.g., the Perceptual Awareness Scale and gradual confidence ratings (Ramsøy and Overgaard, 2004 ; Sandberg and Overgaard, 2015 ).

span.label: phenomenal consciousness —distinct-from→ access consciousness
span.quote: Block ( 2005 ) argues that there may be two neural correlates of consciousness: One relating to phenomenal consciousness (the “early” activations), and one relating to access consciousness (the “late” activations).

span.label: RETRACTED (AN ATTRIBUTED VIEW WHOSE CONTENT IS A NEGATION) · prefrontal cortex —causes→ metacognition
span.quote: According to this view, “late” activations are not actual correlates of consciousness, but are confounds associated with metacognition and report (e.g., Aru et al., 2012 ).

span.label: prefrontal cortex —operationalised-as→ access consciousness
span.quote: Block ( 2005 ) argues that there may be two neural correlates of consciousness: One relating to phenomenal consciousness (the “early” activations), and one relating to access consciousness (the “late” activations).

span.label: preconscious —distinct-from→ consciousness
span.quote: Nevertheless, proponents of the opposite view—that consciousness is associated with prefrontal cortex activity—argue that “early” activations in fact represent preconscious states—i.e., information that is not yet conscious (e.g., Lau and Rosenthal, 2011 ).

span.label: contrastive analysis —operationalised-as→ vegetative state
span.quote: Some studies have attempted to contrast healthy subjects with patients in vegetative state or minimally conscious state (Boly et al., 2013 ), although there are a number of problems: Some experiments indicate that not all such patients are unconscious (Owen et al., 2006 ), and—at the same time—most brain injured patients have many different lesions and, consequently, massive reorganization, which makes comparisons very difficult.

span.label: artificial systems —distinct-from→ consciousness
span.quote: It will very likely be an even greater challenge for a future science of consciousness to consider how to evaluate whether artificial systems (e.g., computers or robots) can be conscious or whether experience is a privilege for biological creatures.

span.label: neural correlate of consciousness —distinct-from→ mind-brain
span.quote: In and of itself, it seems not to be the case that evidence that perceptual experience is associated with—say—activity in primary visual cortex also provides evidence to determine whether consciousness should be seen as—say—identical to or metaphysically different from brain activity.

span.label: confidence ratings —operationalised-as→ subjective report
span.quote: Proponents of the “direct” approach have attempted to develop precise and sensitive scales to capture minor variations in subjective experience, e.g., the Perceptual Awareness Scale and gradual confidence ratings (Ramsøy and Overgaard, 2004 ; Sandberg and Overgaard, 2015 ).

span.label: The field's two dominant problems are not independent: neural correlates cannot be identified without first committing to a measure of consciousness, so the measurement problem is prior to the correlate problem.
span.quote: This challenge clearly relates to the first as one needs to apply a measure of consciousness in order to identify its correlates.

span.label: Objective (indirect) measures cannot escape the weaknesses of introspective report, because calibrating any objective measure requires pairing a behaviour with a subjective report in the first place.
span.quote: This would typically involve associating a subjective report with a particular behavior—a process by which one would “import” all the weaknesses related to subjective reports that one tried to avoid in the first place

span.label: So-called no-report paradigms introduce nothing that escapes introspection either, since the link between the objective marker and conscious experience can only be established by direct introspective report.
span.quote: the only way one may associate a phenomenon as nystagmus with conscious experience is by the direct use of introspection

span.label: Which measurement method is used determines which answer is obtained about the neural correlates of consciousness: some methods yield prefrontal correlates of visual consciousness, others yield occipital/parietal correlates without prefrontal involvement.
span.quote: Whereas this is most likely what is necessary, it is important to notice that different methods seem to generate different results, so that some methods are associated with the finding that the neural correlates of visual consciousness involve prefrontal activity, whereas other methods are associated with the finding that visual consciousness mainly involve occipital/parietal activity but not prefrontal.

span.label: Recent reviews favour the view that consciousness is associated with early occipital/parietal activation rather than late prefrontal activation, with late activity treated as a confound of metacognition and report.
span.quote: According to most recent reviews and articles, evidence is lending support toward the latter view

span.label: Empirical consciousness data currently do not discriminate between metaphysical positions, because existing findings can be accommodated by every theory of the mind-brain relation.
span.quote: Existing data, however, seems to fit easily into every theoretical understanding of this problem.

span.label: The next major challenge the author identifies is measuring consciousness "from the outside" - in non-responsive coma and vegetative-state patients, who have a neural system but no report, and in artificial systems, which may report but have no biological neural system.
span.quote: One major future challenge will be how to measure consciousness “from the outside.”

span.label: Despite these unsolved foundations, consciousness research already works as a discipline producing meaningful and reproducible results.
span.quote: Consciousness research has proven to be an actual and functioning discipline able to provide meaningful and reproducible results.

span.label: different methods of measuring consciousness yield different conclusions about which brain regions are its correlates
span.quote: Whereas this is most likely what is necessary, it is important to notice that different methods seem to generate different results, so that some methods are associated with the finding that the neural correlates of visual consciousness involve prefrontal activity, whereas other methods are associated with the finding that visual consciousness mainly involve occipital/parietal activity but not prefrontal.

span.label: recent reviews favour the occipital/parietal reading over the prefrontal one
span.quote: According to most recent reviews and articles, evidence is lending support toward the latter view (Andersen et al., 2016 ; Koch et al., 2016 ; Hurme et al., 2017 ).

span.label: the same early activations are read as the correlate of consciousness by one camp and as preconscious by the other
span.quote: Nevertheless, proponents of the opposite view—that consciousness is associated with prefrontal cortex activity—argue that “early” activations in fact represent preconscious states—i.e., information that is not yet conscious (e.g., Lau and Rosenthal, 2011 ).

span.label: the existing evidence is compatible with every metaphysical position, so it settles none of them
span.quote: Existing data, however, seems to fit easily into every theoretical understanding of this problem.

span.label: the field has produced meaningful and reproducible results while its central questions remain open
span.quote: Consciousness research has proven to be an actual and functioning discipline able to provide meaningful and reproducible results.

span.label: neural correlate of consciousness (content-specific sense)
span.quote: most experiments aim to identify the minimal neural activations that are sufficient for a specific content of consciousness

span.label: neural correlates of consciousness "as such" (level, not content)
span.term: neural correlates of consciousness "as such" (level, not content)
span.quote: Contrary to this, other scientists are preoccupied with finding neural correlates of consciousness “as such”—i.e., neural correlates that mark the difference between being dead, asleep, awake, etc., and which are not content-specific in the sense above.

span.label: direct approach to measuring consciousness
span.quote: Direct approaches, at least intuitively, are the most informative as participating experimental subjects here simply report about their own experiences.

span.label: indirect (objective-measure) approach
span.quote: Experiments on consciousness that are based on objective measures—the “indirect” approach—typically involve asking subjects to choose between alternatives, e.g., in forced-choice tasks.

span.label: no-report paradigm
span.quote: Nevertheless, experiments of this kind attempt first to associate a particular objective measure (e.g., a behavior or a brain activation) with conscious experience, and then to apply this measure as a measure of consciousness so that no direct report is needed

span.label: REF-CON model of consciousness
span.quote: According to the REF-CON model of consciousness, subjective experience is intrinsically related to a particular kind of “strategy” that makes information available for action

span.label: subjectivity of consciousness (privileged first-person access)
span.quote: Scientists across disciplines generally agree that consciousness is subjective, characterized by a kind of privileged first-person access.

span.label: neural correlate of consciousness
span.quote: most experiments aim to identify the minimal neural activations that are sufficient for a specific content of consciousness (Chalmers, 2000 )

span.label: consciousness as such
span.quote: neural correlates that mark the difference between being dead, asleep, awake, etc., and which are not content-specific in the sense above

span.label: no-report paradigms
span.quote: experiments of this kind attempt first to associate a particular objective measure (e.g., a behavior or a brain activation) with conscious experience, and then to apply this measure as a measure of consciousness so that no direct report is needed

span.label: REF-CON model
span.quote: subjective experience is intrinsically related to a particular kind of “strategy” that makes information available for action
